brainNotes.name: Hamilton, Federalist No. 1 General Introduction
brainNotes.what: Written by Hamilton under the name Publius for the Independent Journal on 27 October 1787, addressed to the people of New York. It argues that the choice about the new Constitution is a test of whether people can build good government by reflection and choice. It warns that interest, ambition and party passion will distort the debate, and Hamilton declares he favors adoption. The essay runs in this order: the importance of the question, the obstacles of self-interest, a call for moderation and candor, the danger of demagogues, Hamilton's own stance, an outline of six topics, and the first topic, the Union.

brainNotes.name: Publius
brainNotes.what: The pen name signed at the end of the essay. The author here is Hamilton, who writes to the people of New York in the first person.

brainNotes.name: Alexander Hamilton
brainNotes.what: The essay is headed HAMILTON as its author. He says he has examined the Constitution and is convinced it is in the people's interest to adopt it. He promises to give his arguments openly while keeping his motives private.

brainNotes.name: Union
brainNotes.what: The joined thirteen States under one general government. Hamilton says its existence is at stake in the debate. He warns that opponents are quietly saying the States are too large for one system and should form separate confederacies. He argues the real choice is the Constitution or dismemberment of the Union.

brainNotes.name: Constitution of 1787
brainNotes.what: The plan for a new national government put before the people for deliberation. Hamilton says it touches many particular interests and local institutions, so it will meet obstacles beyond its merits. He supports its adoption.

brainNotes.name: Articles of Confederation
brainNotes.what: The existing federal government. Hamilton refers to experience showing its inefficacy and promises to show that it is insufficient to preserve the Union.

brainNotes.name: Good government from reflection and choice
aliases: reflection and choice versus accident and force
brainNotes.what: Hamilton asks whether societies can create good government by reflection and choice, or are destined to rely on accident and force. He says America's decision will answer this question for humanity.

brainNotes.name: Interest and ambition as obstacles
brainNotes.what: Hamilton names two groups who will resist the Constitution. One is officeholders under the state establishments who fear losing power and income. The other is ambitious men who hope to gain from confusion or from the split of the empire into partial confederacies. He then concedes that much opposition comes from honest error, jealousy and fear.

brainNotes.name: Moderation and candor in debate
brainNotes.what: Hamilton argues that wise people can be wrong and that supporters can have impure motives too. So everyone should be moderate and avoid intolerance, since persecution does not cure error in politics or in religion. He still predicts angry invective from both sides.

brainNotes.name: Energy of government and liberty
brainNotes.what: Hamilton claims that vigor and efficiency in government are essential to the security of liberty, and the two interests cannot be separated. Supporters of strong government will be called despots, and zealous defenders of rights will be called insincere. He says that dangerous ambition more often hides behind zeal for the people's rights.

brainNotes.name: Demagogues and tyrants
brainNotes.what: Hamilton says history shows that most who overturned republican liberties began by flattering the people. Courting the people is a surer road to despotism than zeal for firm government.

brainNotes.name: Separate confederacies
brainNotes.what: The alternative that some opponents propose: several regional confederacies instead of one union. Hamilton says they argue the thirteen States are too extensive for one general system. He says the real alternative to the Constitution is dismemberment.

brainNotes.name: Plan of the Federalist series
brainNotes.what: Hamilton lists the topics he will discuss: the utility of the Union to political prosperity, the insufficiency of the Confederation, the need for equally energetic government, the conformity of the Constitution to republican principles, its analogy to the New York constitution, and the added security for republican government, liberty and property. He also promises to answer objections.

brainNotes.name: State of New York
brainNotes.what: The audience of the essay, addressed as the people of the State of New York. Hamilton says the Constitution is analogous to their own state constitution.

brainNotes.name: Madison, Federalist No. 10 (The Union as a Safeguard Against Domestic Faction and Insurrection)
brainNotes.what: Madison argues that the Union's chief merit is its tendency to break and control the violence of faction, the fatal disease of popular governments. Faction's causes cannot be removed without destroying liberty, so only its effects can be controlled. A representative republic, especially a large one like the Union, does this best. Structure: the problem of faction (1-3); definition and remedies (4); causes in human nature and property (5-8); only effects can be controlled (9-11); pure democracy versus republic (12-13); two differences, representation and extent (14-17); application to the Union and conclusion (18-19).

brainNotes.name: faction
brainNotes.what: A number of citizens, whether a majority or a minority, united by a common passion or interest opposed to the rights of other citizens or to the community's permanent and aggregate interests. Madison calls it the dangerous vice of popular governments, producing instability, injustice and confusion.

brainNotes.name: two methods of curing faction
brainNotes.what: Faction can be cured by removing its causes or by controlling its effects. Removing causes could be done by destroying liberty or by giving everyone the same opinions, passions and interests. Madison rejects both as unwise or impracticable, leaving control of effects.

brainNotes.name: liberty is to faction what air is to fire
brainNotes.what: Madison's analogy: liberty feeds faction as air feeds fire. Abolishing liberty to end faction would be as foolish as abolishing air to prevent fire, since liberty is essential to political life.

brainNotes.name: causes of faction
brainNotes.what: The causes are sown in human nature: fallible reason joined to self-love, differing opinions, passions, attachments to leaders, even frivolous distinctions. The most common and durable cause is the unequal distribution of property, which flows from the diverse faculties of men.

brainNotes.name: unequal distribution of property
aliases: diversity in the faculties of men
brainNotes.what: Different faculties for acquiring property produce different degrees and kinds of property, and thus different interests: propertied and propertyless, creditors and debtors, landed, manufacturing, mercantile and moneyed interests. Protecting these faculties is government's first object.

brainNotes.name: interests and legislation
aliases: no man a judge in his own cause
brainNotes.what: Regulating the various interfering interests is the main task of modern legislation, which makes party spirit part of ordinary government. Legislators act as parties and judges in their own causes, as on debts, trade restrictions and tax apportionment, so the most numerous faction tends to prevail.

brainNotes.name: controlling the effects of faction
brainNotes.what: Since causes cannot be removed, relief lies in controlling effects. A minority faction is defeated by majority vote under the republican principle. A majority faction is the danger, since popular form lets it sacrifice public good and others' rights. Either the same passion must be prevented in a majority, or the majority must be unable to act in concert.

brainNotes.name: majority faction
brainNotes.what: A faction that includes a majority can use popular government's form to sacrifice the public good and minority rights. Moral and religious motives cannot be relied on to restrain it when impulse and opportunity coincide.

brainNotes.name: pure democracy
brainNotes.what: A society of a small number of citizens who assemble and administer government in person. Madison says it offers no cure for faction, since a majority will share a common passion and nothing checks sacrificing the weaker party. Such democracies were turbulent, insecure for property and short-lived.

brainNotes.name: republic
brainNotes.what: A government in which representation takes place. It differs from democracy by delegating government to a small number of elected citizens and by extending over a greater number of citizens and sphere of country. Madison holds it promises the cure for faction.

brainNotes.name: representatives as refining public views
brainNotes.what: Passing public opinion through a chosen body may refine and enlarge it, so the public voice may better serve the public good than the people themselves would. But factious or corrupt men might win office and betray the people, so the question becomes whether small or large republics choose better guardians.

brainNotes.name: extending the sphere
brainNotes.what: A larger republic has more citizens and a greater variety of parties and interests. A majority is less likely to share a common motive, and it is harder for those who do to discover their strength and act together. Larger electorates also make it harder for unworthy candidates to win.

brainNotes.name: federal Constitution's division of interests
brainNotes.what: Madison says there is a mean in the number of electors: too many leaves representatives ignorant of local interests, too few leaves them parochial. The federal Constitution combines both by assigning great aggregate interests to the national government and local ones to State legislatures.

brainNotes.name: paper money, abolition of debts, equal division of property
brainNotes.what: Madison's examples of improper or wicked projects that a faction might pursue. They are more likely to infect a county or State than the whole Union.

brainNotes.name: Federalists
brainNotes.what: Supporters of the proposed Constitution. Madison closes saying that to the degree we take pleasure and pride in being republicans, we should be zealous in supporting the character of Federalists.

brainNotes.name: Madison
brainNotes.what: Author of Federalist No. 10, as the file labels it, writing to the people of New York. He argues faction is inevitable and best checked by a large representative republic.

brainNotes.name: Lecture 3 slides
brainNotes.what: Slide deck for Week 3 arguing, from Federalist No. 51, that good people cannot be simply trusted and that government's structure must itself restrain power. It moves from the problem (power gathers, written limits fail), to separate departments, ambition against ambition, dividing the legislature, the veto, the double division between national and state government, and a link back to faction (No. 10). It ends with seminar questions.

brainNotes.name: Federalist No. 51
brainNotes.what: The Federalist paper that is the source text for the lecture. It argues that the structure of government, not trust in good people, must keep power in check through separate departments and divided authority.

brainNotes.name: Checks and balances
brainNotes.what: The idea that government's structure should resist the gathering of power, because written limits alone will not hold. Branches are arranged so each can restrain the others.

brainNotes.name: Separation of powers
brainNotes.what: Government is divided into legislative, executive and judicial departments. Each draws its power from a different source and needs some independence from the others.

brainNotes.name: Concentration of power
brainNotes.what: The problem that power tends to gather in one place. The lecture says written limits alone will not stop this, so the structure must resist it.

brainNotes.name: Ambition against ambition
brainNotes.what: Each officeholder is given a personal stake in the office. The interest of the person is tied to the rights of the place, so self-interest defends each branch.

brainNotes.name: Dividing the legislature
brainNotes.what: The legislature is the strongest branch, so it is split into two houses with different modes of election. Weakness in one branch is covered by the others.

brainNotes.name: The veto
brainNotes.what: A qualified executive veto defends the executive against the legislature. It also checks hasty law.

brainNotes.name: Double security
brainNotes.what: Power is split between national and state governments, and then each government is split again. Rights thereby get a double security.

brainNotes.name: Federalist No. 10
brainNotes.what: The Federalist paper on faction, which the lecture asks students to compare with No. 51.

brainNotes.name: Justice as the end of government
brainNotes.what: The lecture states that justice is the end of government. A society of many interests protects minorities toward that end.

brainNotes.name: Madison, Federalist No. 51
brainNotes.what: Madison (writing as Publius) argues that since parchment or exterior provisions cannot keep the departments of government separate, the government's interior structure must make the parts check each other. He argues for departments with wills of their own, ambition set against ambition, a divided legislature and a fortified executive. He then argues that the compound federal republic gives double security, and that a large, diverse society protects minority rights. Structure: (1) the problem and the proposed remedy; (2) independence of departments in appointment and pay; (3) ambition countering ambition and the angels passage; (4) the legislature's predominance and the remedies; (5) two considerations special to the federal system: double security and protection against majority faction; (6) justice, Rhode Island and the extended republic.

brainNotes.name: Interior structure of government
brainNotes.what: Madison's answer to the failure of exterior provisions: design the government so that its constituent parts, through their mutual relations, keep each other in their proper places.

brainNotes.name: Each department should have a will of its own
brainNotes.what: Each department should have as little agency as possible in appointing members of the others. Strictly, all appointments would come from the people through separate channels. Madison admits deviations because of difficulty and expense.

brainNotes.name: Judiciary department
brainNotes.what: Madison says the strict principle of separate appointment need not apply fully to the judiciary. Judges need special qualifications, and permanent tenure soon destroys any sense of dependence on the appointing authority. Judges and the executive must also not depend on the legislature for their pay, or their independence would be merely nominal.

brainNotes.name: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition
brainNotes.what: The principle that the interest of the officeholder should be tied to the constitutional rights of his office. Self-interest and rival interests then resist encroachment by other departments. This supplies the defect of better motives.

brainNotes.name: If men were angels
brainNotes.what: Madison says that if men were angels, no government would be necessary, and if angels governed men, no controls would be needed. Because men govern men, the government must first control the governed and then be obliged to control itself.

brainNotes.name: Auxiliary precautions
brainNotes.what: Dependence on the people is the primary control on government. Experience has shown the need for extra safeguards beyond it, such as the internal checks among departments.

brainNotes.name: Legislative predominance
brainNotes.what: In a republic the legislative authority necessarily predominates, so departments cannot have equal power of self-defense. Madison proposes dividing the legislature into branches with different modes of election and principles of action. He proposes fortifying the weaker executive, perhaps by a qualified connection with the weaker legislative branch rather than an absolute veto.

brainNotes.name: Absolute negative
brainNotes.what: An absolute executive veto on the legislature is the natural defense for the executive. Madison thinks it is neither safe nor sufficient, because it might not be used firmly in ordinary times and might be abused in extraordinary times.

brainNotes.name: Compound republic
brainNotes.what: In America, the power surrendered by the people is first divided between two governments (national and state). Each portion is then subdivided among separate departments. This produces a double security for the rights of the people, because the governments control each other and each controls itself.

brainNotes.name: Protection of minority rights against majority
brainNotes.what: A republic must guard one part of society against injustice from another. If a majority is united by a common interest, minority rights are insecure. There are two remedies: an independent will in the community, which is precarious, or so many different kinds of citizens that an unjust majority is improbable.

brainNotes.name: Multiplicity of interests and sects
brainNotes.what: Civil rights are secured by a multiplicity of interests, just as religious rights are secured by a multiplicity of sects. The degree of security depends on their number, which depends on the size of the country and population.

brainNotes.name: Extended republic
brainNotes.what: Madison argues that the larger the society, within a practical sphere, the better it can govern itself. A majority coalition in a large and varied society would seldom form on any principles other than justice and the general good. Smaller confederacies would make oppressive majorities easier.

brainNotes.name: Federal principle
brainNotes.what: The federal principle, judiciously modified and mixed, allows the practicable sphere of a republic to extend very far. Madison says this serves the republican cause.

brainNotes.name: Justice
brainNotes.what: Madison says justice is the end of government and civil society, and is pursued until obtained or until liberty is lost. A society where the stronger faction can oppress the weaker is as anarchic as a state of nature. Powerful factions too would come to want a government that protects all.

brainNotes.name: Rhode Island
brainNotes.what: Madison uses Rhode Island as a hypothetical example. If it were separated from the Confederacy, the oppressions of factious majorities within its narrow limits would lead the factions themselves to call for a power independent of the people.

brainMentions.what: Written by Hamilton under the name Publius for the Independent Journal on 27 October 1787, addressed to the people of New York. It argues that the choice about the new Constitution is a test of whether people can build good government by reflection and choice. It warns that interest, ambition and party passion will distort the debate, and Hamilton declares he favors adoption. The essay runs in this order: the importance of the question, the obstacles of self-interest, a call for moderation and candor, the danger of demagogues, Hamilton's own stance, an outline of six topics, and the first topic, the Union.
brainMentions.why: It frames the whole series and gives its plan, so it is the starting point for the course.

brainMentions.what: The pen name signed at the end of the essay. The author here is Hamilton, who writes to the people of New York in the first person.
brainMentions.why: It is the voice that argues for the Constitution across the series.

brainMentions.what: The essay is headed HAMILTON as its author. He says he has examined the Constitution and is convinced it is in the people's interest to adopt it. He promises to give his arguments openly while keeping his motives private.
brainMentions.why: He opens the series and sets out its purpose and plan.

brainMentions.what: The joined thirteen States under one general government. Hamilton says its existence is at stake in the debate. He warns that opponents are quietly saying the States are too large for one system and should form separate confederacies. He argues the real choice is the Constitution or dismemberment of the Union.
brainMentions.why: The utility of the Union is the first topic of the series and the subject of the next essay.

brainMentions.what: The plan for a new national government put before the people for deliberation. Hamilton says it touches many particular interests and local institutions, so it will meet obstacles beyond its merits. He supports its adoption.
brainMentions.why: It is the document the whole series defends.

brainMentions.what: The existing federal government. Hamilton refers to experience showing its inefficacy and promises to show that it is insufficient to preserve the Union.
brainMentions.why: Its failure is the reason a new government is needed.

brainMentions.what: Hamilton asks whether societies can create good government by reflection and choice, or are destined to rely on accident and force. He says America's decision will answer this question for humanity.
brainMentions.why: It gives the stakes of ratification as a test for self-government.

brainMentions.what: Hamilton names two groups who will resist the Constitution. One is officeholders under the state establishments who fear losing power and income. The other is ambitious men who hope to gain from confusion or from the split of the empire into partial confederacies. He then concedes that much opposition comes from honest error, jealousy and fear.
brainMentions.why: It shows his awareness of motives and his call for candor.

brainMentions.what: Hamilton argues that wise people can be wrong and that supporters can have impure motives too. So everyone should be moderate and avoid intolerance, since persecution does not cure error in politics or in religion. He still predicts angry invective from both sides.
brainMentions.why: It sets the tone he wants for the ratification debate.

brainMentions.what: Hamilton claims that vigor and efficiency in government are essential to the security of liberty, and the two interests cannot be separated. Supporters of strong government will be called despots, and zealous defenders of rights will be called insincere. He says that dangerous ambition more often hides behind zeal for the people's rights.
brainMentions.why: It is his central claim for a strong national government.

brainMentions.what: Hamilton says history shows that most who overturned republican liberties began by flattering the people. Courting the people is a surer road to despotism than zeal for firm government.
brainMentions.why: It warns against opponents who pose as defenders of the people.

brainMentions.what: The alternative that some opponents propose: several regional confederacies instead of one union. Hamilton says they argue the thirteen States are too extensive for one general system. He says the real alternative to the Constitution is dismemberment.
brainMentions.why: It is the danger that makes examining the Union necessary.

brainMentions.what: Hamilton lists the topics he will discuss: the utility of the Union to political prosperity, the insufficiency of the Confederation, the need for equally energetic government, the conformity of the Constitution to republican principles, its analogy to the New York constitution, and the added security for republican government, liberty and property. He also promises to answer objections.
brainMentions.why: It is the roadmap for the course readings.

brainMentions.what: The audience of the essay, addressed as the people of the State of New York. Hamilton says the Constitution is analogous to their own state constitution.
brainMentions.why: It identifies who must be persuaded to ratify.

brainMentions.what: Madison argues that the Union's chief merit is its tendency to break and control the violence of faction, the fatal disease of popular governments. Faction's causes cannot be removed without destroying liberty, so only its effects can be controlled. A representative republic, especially a large one like the Union, does this best. Structure: the problem of faction (1-3); definition and remedies (4); causes in human nature and property (5-8); only effects can be controlled (9-11); pure democracy versus republic (12-13); two differences, representation and extent (14-17); application to the Union and conclusion (18-19).
brainMentions.why: It is the week's core text on faction and the large republic, and it justifies the Constitution's extended Union.

brainMentions.what: A number of citizens, whether a majority or a minority, united by a common passion or interest opposed to the rights of other citizens or to the community's permanent and aggregate interests. Madison calls it the dangerous vice of popular governments, producing instability, injustice and confusion.
brainMentions.why: It is the central problem Federalist 10 seeks to cure.

brainMentions.what: Faction can be cured by removing its causes or by controlling its effects. Removing causes could be done by destroying liberty or by giving everyone the same opinions, passions and interests. Madison rejects both as unwise or impracticable, leaving control of effects.
brainMentions.why: It structures the argument and leads to the republican solution.
related: liberty is to faction what air is to fire

brainMentions.what: Madison's analogy: liberty feeds faction as air feeds fire. Abolishing liberty to end faction would be as foolish as abolishing air to prevent fire, since liberty is essential to political life.
brainMentions.why: It explains why the first way of removing causes is rejected as worse than the disease.

brainMentions.what: The causes are sown in human nature: fallible reason joined to self-love, differing opinions, passions, attachments to leaders, even frivolous distinctions. The most common and durable cause is the unequal distribution of property, which flows from the diverse faculties of men.
brainMentions.why: Because they are rooted in human nature, they cannot be removed, so effects must be controlled.

brainMentions.what: Different faculties for acquiring property produce different degrees and kinds of property, and thus different interests: propertied and propertyless, creditors and debtors, landed, manufacturing, mercantile and moneyed interests. Protecting these faculties is government's first object.
brainMentions.why: It is Madison's most common and durable source of faction.

brainMentions.what: Regulating the various interfering interests is the main task of modern legislation, which makes party spirit part of ordinary government. Legislators act as parties and judges in their own causes, as on debts, trade restrictions and tax apportionment, so the most numerous faction tends to prevail.
brainMentions.why: It shows faction is built into ordinary lawmaking and enlightened statesmen cannot be relied on.

brainMentions.what: Since causes cannot be removed, relief lies in controlling effects. A minority faction is defeated by majority vote under the republican principle. A majority faction is the danger, since popular form lets it sacrifice public good and others' rights. Either the same passion must be prevented in a majority, or the majority must be unable to act in concert.
brainMentions.why: It frames the great object of Madison's inquiry.

brainMentions.what: A faction that includes a majority can use popular government's form to sacrifice the public good and minority rights. Moral and religious motives cannot be relied on to restrain it when impulse and opportunity coincide.
brainMentions.why: It is the specific danger the large republic is meant to solve.

brainMentions.what: A society of a small number of citizens who assemble and administer government in person. Madison says it offers no cure for faction, since a majority will share a common passion and nothing checks sacrificing the weaker party. Such democracies were turbulent, insecure for property and short-lived.
brainMentions.why: It is the foil against which the republic is defined.

brainMentions.what: A government in which representation takes place. It differs from democracy by delegating government to a small number of elected citizens and by extending over a greater number of citizens and sphere of country. Madison holds it promises the cure for faction.
brainMentions.why: It is Madison's proposed remedy.

brainMentions.what: Passing public opinion through a chosen body may refine and enlarge it, so the public voice may better serve the public good than the people themselves would. But factious or corrupt men might win office and betray the people, so the question becomes whether small or large republics choose better guardians.
brainMentions.why: It is the first difference between republic and democracy.

brainMentions.what: A larger republic has more citizens and a greater variety of parties and interests. A majority is less likely to share a common motive, and it is harder for those who do to discover their strength and act together. Larger electorates also make it harder for unworthy candidates to win.
brainMentions.why: It is the book's famous central claim, that the large republic best controls faction.

brainMentions.what: The Union is the larger republic. Its representatives are likelier to be enlightened, its variety of parties greater, and its obstacles to unjust majorities larger than in any one State. Factious flames, sects or rages for paper money or debt abolition would stay local rather than spread.
brainMentions.why: It applies the argument to the proposed Constitution and justifies Federalism.

brainMentions.what: Madison says there is a mean in the number of electors: too many leaves representatives ignorant of local interests, too few leaves them parochial. The federal Constitution combines both by assigning great aggregate interests to the national government and local ones to State legislatures.
brainMentions.why: It shows how the Constitution balances national and local concerns.

brainMentions.what: Madison's examples of improper or wicked projects that a faction might pursue. They are more likely to infect a county or State than the whole Union.
brainMentions.why: They illustrate the dangers the large republic contains.

brainMentions.what: Supporters of the proposed Constitution. Madison closes saying that to the degree we take pleasure and pride in being republicans, we should be zealous in supporting the character of Federalists.
brainMentions.why: It ties the republican remedy to support for ratification.

brainMentions.what: Author of Federalist No. 10, as the file labels it, writing to the people of New York. He argues faction is inevitable and best checked by a large representative republic.
brainMentions.why: He supplies the argument studied this week.

brainMentions.what: The shared pseudonym under which the Federalist essay is signed.
brainMentions.why: It is the signature of the essay in the file.

brainMentions.what: The state whose people the essay addresses, as published in the Daily Advertiser on November 22, 1787.
brainMentions.why: It identifies the audience in the ratification debate.

brainMentions.what: Slide deck for Week 3 arguing, from Federalist No. 51, that good people cannot be simply trusted and that government's structure must itself restrain power. It moves from the problem (power gathers, written limits fail), to separate departments, ambition against ambition, dividing the legislature, the veto, the double division between national and state government, and a link back to faction (No. 10). It ends with seminar questions.
brainMentions.why: It is the course's Week 3 overview of separation of powers and checks and balances.

brainMentions.what: The Federalist paper that is the source text for the lecture. It argues that the structure of government, not trust in good people, must keep power in check through separate departments and divided authority.
brainMentions.why: It is the central document of the lecture.

brainMentions.what: The idea that government's structure should resist the gathering of power, because written limits alone will not hold. Branches are arranged so each can restrain the others.
brainMentions.why: It is the lecture's main topic and answers the question of why not just trust good people.

brainMentions.what: Government is divided into legislative, executive and judicial departments. Each draws its power from a different source and needs some independence from the others.
brainMentions.why: It is the first structural safeguard against concentrated power.

brainMentions.what: The problem that power tends to gather in one place. The lecture says written limits alone will not stop this, so the structure must resist it.
brainMentions.why: It is the problem that motivates the whole design.

brainMentions.what: Each officeholder is given a personal stake in the office. The interest of the person is tied to the rights of the place, so self-interest defends each branch.
brainMentions.why: It explains how checks work without relying on virtue; the seminar questions whether it is reliable.

brainMentions.what: The legislature is the strongest branch, so it is split into two houses with different modes of election. Weakness in one branch is covered by the others.
brainMentions.why: It shows how the strongest branch is restrained internally.

brainMentions.what: A qualified executive veto defends the executive against the legislature. It also checks hasty law.
brainMentions.why: It is the example of a check that gives the executive a defense.

brainMentions.what: Power is split between national and state governments, and then each government is split again. Rights thereby get a double security.
brainMentions.why: It adds a second layer of protection beyond separation of powers.

brainMentions.what: The slide returns to faction: a society of many interests protects minorities. It says justice is the end of government.
brainMentions.why: It links No. 51 to No. 10 and to the argument from size.

brainMentions.what: The Federalist paper on faction, which the lecture asks students to compare with No. 51.
brainMentions.why: It supplies the faction argument that complements the structural one.

brainMentions.what: The lecture states that justice is the end of government. A society of many interests protects minorities toward that end.
brainMentions.why: It states the purpose the structures serve.

brainMentions.what: Madison (writing as Publius) argues that since parchment or exterior provisions cannot keep the departments of government separate, the government's interior structure must make the parts check each other. He argues for departments with wills of their own, ambition set against ambition, a divided legislature and a fortified executive. He then argues that the compound federal republic gives double security, and that a large, diverse society protects minority rights. Structure: (1) the problem and the proposed remedy; (2) independence of departments in appointment and pay; (3) ambition countering ambition and the angels passage; (4) the legislature's predominance and the remedies; (5) two considerations special to the federal system: double security and protection against majority faction; (6) justice, Rhode Island and the extended republic.
brainMentions.why: It is the core Week 3 text on separation of powers and checks and balances.
related: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition

brainMentions.what: The division of government power among distinct executive, legislative and judiciary departments, which is admitted to be essential to liberty. Madison says that the written division in the Constitution is not enough to maintain it in practice.
brainMentions.why: It is the problem the essay sets out to solve.
related: Each department should have a will of its own

brainMentions.what: The arrangement in which each department has the constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachments by the others. The parts of government keep each other in their places through their mutual relations.
brainMentions.why: It is the essay's central remedy for the concentration of power.
related: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition

brainMentions.what: Madison's answer to the failure of exterior provisions: design the government so that its constituent parts, through their mutual relations, keep each other in their proper places.
brainMentions.why: It is the thesis of the opening paragraph and the basis of everything that follows.

brainMentions.what: Each department should have as little agency as possible in appointing members of the others. Strictly, all appointments would come from the people through separate channels. Madison admits deviations because of difficulty and expense.
brainMentions.why: It is the foundation for departmental independence, with admitted exceptions.

brainMentions.what: Madison says the strict principle of separate appointment need not apply fully to the judiciary. Judges need special qualifications, and permanent tenure soon destroys any sense of dependence on the appointing authority. Judges and the executive must also not depend on the legislature for their pay, or their independence would be merely nominal.
brainMentions.why: It shows the exceptions Madison allows to the independence principle.
related: Each department should have a will of its own

brainMentions.what: The principle that the interest of the officeholder should be tied to the constitutional rights of his office. Self-interest and rival interests then resist encroachment by other departments. This supplies the defect of better motives.
brainMentions.why: It is the best-known statement of Madison's psychology of checks.

brainMentions.what: Madison says that if men were angels, no government would be necessary, and if angels governed men, no controls would be needed. Because men govern men, the government must first control the governed and then be obliged to control itself.
brainMentions.why: It states his view of human nature and why government needs internal controls.
related: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition

brainMentions.what: Dependence on the people is the primary control on government. Experience has shown the need for extra safeguards beyond it, such as the internal checks among departments.
brainMentions.why: It explains why elections alone are not enough.

brainMentions.what: In a republic the legislative authority necessarily predominates, so departments cannot have equal power of self-defense. Madison proposes dividing the legislature into branches with different modes of election and principles of action. He proposes fortifying the weaker executive, perhaps by a qualified connection with the weaker legislative branch rather than an absolute veto.
brainMentions.why: It explains why bicameralism and an executive check are needed.

brainMentions.what: An absolute executive veto on the legislature is the natural defense for the executive. Madison thinks it is neither safe nor sufficient, because it might not be used firmly in ordinary times and might be abused in extraordinary times.
brainMentions.why: It shows Madison weighing the executive's defenses.

brainMentions.what: In America, the power surrendered by the people is first divided between two governments (national and state). Each portion is then subdivided among separate departments. This produces a double security for the rights of the people, because the governments control each other and each controls itself.
brainMentions.why: It is the first consideration specific to the American federal system.

brainMentions.what: A republic must guard one part of society against injustice from another. If a majority is united by a common interest, minority rights are insecure. There are two remedies: an independent will in the community, which is precarious, or so many different kinds of citizens that an unjust majority is improbable.
brainMentions.why: It is the second consideration and leads to the extended republic argument.

brainMentions.what: Civil rights are secured by a multiplicity of interests, just as religious rights are secured by a multiplicity of sects. The degree of security depends on their number, which depends on the size of the country and population.
brainMentions.why: It is the mechanism by which a large republic protects minorities.
related: Protection of minority rights against majority

brainMentions.what: Madison argues that the larger the society, within a practical sphere, the better it can govern itself. A majority coalition in a large and varied society would seldom form on any principles other than justice and the general good. Smaller confederacies would make oppressive majorities easier.
brainMentions.why: It is the essay's conclusion and defense of the large federal Union.

brainMentions.what: The federal principle, judiciously modified and mixed, allows the practicable sphere of a republic to extend very far. Madison says this serves the republican cause.
brainMentions.why: It is the closing point of the essay.

brainMentions.what: Madison says justice is the end of government and civil society, and is pursued until obtained or until liberty is lost. A society where the stronger faction can oppress the weaker is as anarchic as a state of nature. Powerful factions too would come to want a government that protects all.
brainMentions.why: It is the moral goal behind the structural arguments.
related: Protection of minority rights against majority

brainMentions.what: Madison uses Rhode Island as a hypothetical example. If it were separated from the Confederacy, the oppressions of factious majorities within its narrow limits would lead the factions themselves to call for a power independent of the people.
brainMentions.why: It illustrates the danger of small republics.

brainMentions.what: Publius is the pseudonym under which the Federalist essays were published. This essay is headed Madison and addressed to the people of the State of New York.
brainMentions.why: He is the essay's author and voice.
